analysis.one_liner: Bans housing, public accommodation, and public facility discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died there when the Congress ended, despite Democrats holding a 253-seat House majority.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added sexual orientation and gender identity to the Fair Housing Act, making it illegal to refuse to sell or rent a home, provide a mortgage, or offer brokerage services to someone because they are gay, lesbian, bisexual, or transgender. It would also have added those categories to the public accommodations and public facilities sections of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, covering hotels, restaurants, and government-run facilities. It was introduced by one New York Democrat with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBT Americans — gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender people — who in most states could be denied an apartment, a mortgage, or a hotel room purely because of who they are, with no federal remedy. In states without their own nondiscrimination laws, the bill would have given them the same federal protections against housing and public-accommodation discrimination that already exist for race, religion, national origin, and sex.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would amend the Fair Housing Act to make it illegal to discriminate based on sexual orientation or gender identity in selling or renting homes, in mortgage and other residential real-estate transactions, and in real-estate brokerage services — the same protections already covering race, religion, national origin, and sex.

It would extend the Civil Rights Act of 1964's public accommodations rules — which govern hotels, restaurants, and similar places open to the public — and its public facilities rules to cover sexual orientation and gender identity.

It would add sexual orientation and gender identity to the Fair Housing Act's provision against intimidating or interfering with a person's housing rights, and it states that nothing in the law requires anyone to disclose their own sexual orientation or gender identity.
The bill directed HUD to issue implementing rules within 180 days of enactment, so the new protections would have taken practical effect quickly.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords, mortgage lenders, and real-estate brokers who would face new federal anti-discrimination obligations and potential complaints if they treated LGBT applicants differently; operators of hotels, restaurants, and other public accommodations who could no longer refuse service to LGBT customers; the public facilities provisions apply mainly to government.

drawbacks.text: The bill would place new legal obligations on landlords, mortgage lenders, brokers, and operators of hotels, restaurants, and other public accommodations in states with no state-level protection, exposing them to federal complaints and litigation if they refuse housing or service on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Critics of extending public-accommodations and housing rules to gender identity have argued in analogous debates that it can conflict with the preferences of private property owners and with sex-segregated facilities, raising religious-liberty and privacy objections that the bill does not carve out.

The bill is drafted as an amendment to existing civil rights statutes, which means its practical reach — including how 'gender identity' is applied in enforcement — would depend heavily on later HUD rulemaking and court interpretation rather than being fully specified in the text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefits for LGBT Americans — equal access to housing, hotels, restaurants, and public buildings under the same federal civil rights framework that already covers race, religion, national origin, and sex — are substantial for a group facing documented housing discrimination, and the bill's costs (compliance by landlords, lenders, and businesses in states without such laws) mirror the costs civil rights laws have always imposed. The honest objections are the religious-liberty and disclosure-privacy concerns, which the bill addressed only partially through its interpretive rule. But the outcome was decided before any of this was debated: with no cosponsors and no committee action, the bill's merits were never tested. The bill's weaknesses as a matter of design are minor; its failure was a matter of support, not substance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2010, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then parked in its civil rights subcommittee, and Congress ended in January 2011 with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Edolphus Towns of New York introduced the Housing Nondiscrimination Act of 2010 in the House on March 11, 2010.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with zero cosponsors.
On April 26, 2010, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties — the last recorded action; it never advanced further.
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords, lenders, and businesses that refuse service to LGBT customers kept the status quo: no federal anti-discrimination duty for sexual orientation or gender identity. No one gained protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords and businesses that refused LGBT customers

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.role: U.S. Representative, New York; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its only sponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Conyers (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, a markup, or a vote from April 2010 until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 26, 2010 and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough for anyone to vote on it, so no party split is recorded; it had a Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, though Democrats held a 253-seat House majority during the session.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from refusing tenants or applying different terms based on sexual orientation or gender identity, a new federal compliance duty in most states. It restricts conduct rather than revenue and applies only to discriminatory decisions.

The Fair Housing Act's real-estate transaction and brokerage provisions would extend to the new categories, subjecting lending and brokerage decisions to anti-discrimination review. Ordinary borrowers and buyers gain protection; the industry bears compliance and liability costs.

industries.industry: Hotels, restaurants, and other public accommodations
industries.note: The Civil Rights Act's public accommodations title would apply to sexual orientation and gender identity, ending lawful refusal of service in states without such laws. The cost to businesses is limited to serving customers they currently may turn away.
